A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Uploading first means the switch is the only step users can observe, and everything it points to is already in place.

We keep the old assets because browsers that loaded the previous manifest still request the old names. A page opened before the switch, or a cached copy of the old manifest, will keep fetching those files for a while. If we deleted them at release time, those users would get errors mid-session. Versioned names make this safe: old and new files never collide, so both releases can be served side by side.

Each release goes out in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned filename (for example, `app.3f9c2.js`), then we switch the manifest so it points at those new names. Previous versions' assets stay where they are.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at something that isn't there yet. The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the upload finished, any browser that fetched it in that gap would request files that don't exist yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means that, from the moment the switch happens, every name in the new manifest already resolves.

We keep the old assets because browsers that loaded the previous manifest still rely on them. A browser that fetched the old manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old versioned names, for example when it lazy-loads a script or stylesheet later in the session. If we deleted those files at the switch, those users would get missing files partway through their visit. Versioned names let old and new sets sit side by side without overwriting each other, so both groups of users get a consistent set of files.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a new versioned filename, then point the manifest at those names. The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live.

The upload comes first because once the manifest changes, browsers immediately start requesting the files it names. If any of those files aren't on the server yet, those requests fail and pages break. Uploading everything first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the manifest goes live. Because the new files have new names, uploading them doesn't touch anything the current site is using.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach everyone at once. A browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the files that manifest named, such as lazy-loaded scripts, images or chunks fetched later in the session. If we deleted those files, users who were mid-session during the release would get errors. Keeping them means both the old and new manifests resolve fully, so a release never breaks anyone's open page.
